theme: Social and moral laws, justice in covenant community
readingInstruction: Read Deuteronomy 22:1-25:19. This is the longest section of specific laws. It covers everyday matters of community life, from lost animals to marriage, to honest weights. Read it as a picture of how God cares about the details of ordinary life.
settingTheScene: These chapters read like a collection of case laws. They touch on how to treat a neighbor’s property, sexual morality, who may belong to the assembly of the LORD, hygiene in the camp, treatment of the poor and the foreigner, marriage and divorce, and business ethics. Some of the laws are hard to understand, as they come from a very different time and culture. But the principles behind them are clear.
observation: “You shall not see your brother’s ox or his sheep going astray, and hide yourselves from them. You shall take them back to your brother” (22:1).
“You shall make a parapet for your roof, that you may not bring the guilt of blood upon your house” (22:8).
“You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together” (22:10).
A man who is newly married is to be free from military service for a year, “to be happy with his wife” (24:5).
“You shall not oppress a hired servant who is poor and needy” (24:14-15).
“Fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers” (24:16).
“When you reap your harvest in your field and forget a sheaf… it shall be for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow” (24:19).
“You shall have a full and just weight, a full and just measure” (25:13-16). “You shall blot out the memory of Amalek” (25:17-19).
interpretation:
The laws of these chapters show the extent of God’s concern. He cares about a lost ox, a house roof, a pair of unlike animals, the wages of a day laborer, the way a person lends, and how fair a merchant’s scale is. Nothing is too small. This is a God who is holy in the market as well as in the temple.

The first law sets the tone: if you see your neighbor’s animal wandering, you must take it back. You cannot say, “It’s not my problem.” To love your neighbor means taking active responsibility for his welfare. The same principle shows up in the roof parapet. Because roofs were used as living space, a house owner has to make them safe. If you build a house, you take responsibility for the safety of anyone who enters it.

Several laws protect the vulnerable. The hired servant must be paid on the same day, because he is poor and depends on the wages. The gleaning laws leave behind some of the harvest for the poor. A creditor may not enter a debtor’s home to take a pledge, nor keep his cloak overnight. Foreigners, widows, and orphans are not to be denied justice. Each of these says, “Remember that you were a slave in Egypt.” Generosity is grounded in redemption.

A line in 24:16 is a landmark: each person is responsible for his own sin. In a world where families were often punished together, this was a significant principle. It shows that God’s justice is personal.

The call for honest weights and measures says that business ethics is a matter of worship. “For all who do such things, all who act dishonestly, are an abomination to the LORD your God.” The God of Israel cares what your scale says.

The section ends with a reminder of Amalek, the nation that attacked the weak and tired at the rear of Israel’s column when they came out of Egypt. This is the theme again: God is the defender of the weak.
connection: Jesus said that the second great commandment is to love your neighbor as yourself, and in the parable of the Good Samaritan he extended “neighbor” to anyone in need (Luke 10:25-37). Paul quotes the law about the ox, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain,” to support paying those who preach (1 Corinthians 9:9). James 5:4 echoes the law about unpaid wages. Jesus’ compassion for the weak, the hungry, and the foreigner is the fulfillment of these laws.
application:
Ask whether there is a “lost ox” in your life, something of a neighbor’s that you could help return.

Review your business and financial dealings. Are your weights and measures honest?

Think about how you treat workers, and whether there is someone you should pay or tip more fairly.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to make you honest, fair, and generous in practical ways.
Tell him one way you want to love a neighbor this week.
